newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-U.S. data drive markets ahead of G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-U.S. data drive markets ahead of G7 summit.

text.p: Financial markets on both sides of the Atlantic reacted strongly on Thursday to U.S. figures showing a rise in weekly jobless claims and a narrower than expected international trade deficit.

The Dow Jones industial average zoomed up 50 points in the first minutes of trade, but a strong June business activity index later helped to clip U.S. bonds and stocks fell back to stand around 28 points up as European bourses closed.
The dollar also leapt on the trade data, climbing through 114 yen and 1.7360 marks but was unable to hang on to its highs against the mark.
By the end of European business, only Frankfurt of the major bourses was showing gains. The London and Paris stock markets ended in the minus column, bedevilled by local concerns.

The U.S. Department of Commerce said the American trade deficit rose 7.8 percent to $8.4 billion in April, but that was lower than expected and, combined with the rise in jobless claims, provided a boost to the markets.

"Exports are showing considerable strength, which is particularly good news in the face of a strong dollar," said Lynn Reaser, chief economist at Barnett Bank Inc in the United States. "It indicates the improvement in various countries throughout the world and that U.S productivity is allowing good export performance."

The trade data came a day after Japan reported a 222 percent rise in its overall trade surplus and the day before the leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations begin a three-day meeting at which trade could become a source of friction.

Most dealers do not expect G7 -- the United States, Canada, Germany, Japan, France, Britain and Italy -- to change its stance on foreign exchange rates from April's statement that opposed wild currency swings.
The dollar has depreciated almost 12 percent from a 4-1/2 year high of 127.47 yen reached just after the last G7 meeting in Washington in April.

German shares proved the strongest among Europe's major equity markets, with dealers saying the market was largely driven by technical factors ahead of Friday's "triple witching" of futures and options contracts.
The Ifo economic institute reported that German business confidence was slightly higher than expected in May and said it believed Europe's powerhouse economy could still qualify for monetary union.
It forecast German gross domestic product would grow between 2.0 and 2.5 percent in 1997, but the average number of unemployed would rise by more than 300,000 to 4.3 million.
The 30-share DAX index closed up 19 points, or 0.51 percent, at 3,749.27 and the IBIS DAX index ended 1.26 percent up in later screen-based business.
French stocks spent a volatile day but slipped as new Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's made his keynote policy speech to parliament.
Declaring that commitments made during the election campaign would be honoured, Jospin announced a modest boost to the minimum wage and a gradual move to a 35-hour week.

Privatisation candidate Thomson-CSF was a big loser at one point after Jospin said the government did not favour selling the state electronic and aerospace firm. But its shares ended up 0.33 percent at 152.4 francs.
The blue-chip CAC-40 index closed down 12.05 points, or 0.44 percent, at 2,739.69.
Like Frankfurt, the London share market was heavily influenced by derivatives ahead of Friday's futures and options expiry.

Also weighing on the market were worries about next month's budget and news of an 11.1 percent year-on-year rise in M4 money supply in May, which reinforced fears of another rise in interest rates following Wednesday's strong retail sales figures.

"The figures today are going to be damaging to the gilt markets with such strong lending on the back of strong retail sales numbers. It is certainly going to put upward pressure on inflation expectations," Nikko economist Simon Briscoe said.
"It is now quite likely that base rates will rise in July unless the budget is especially tough on the personal sector."
The blue chip FTSE 100 index managed to claw back most of its losses by the end, however, and closed just 3.3 points adrift at 4,653.7.
CURRENCIES AT 1600 GMT
The dollar was at 1.7240 marks and 114.13 yen, compared with 1.7289 and 113.32 in late European trade on Wednesday.
STOCK MARKETS -- CLOSING INDICES
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index closed down 3.3 points, or 0.07 percent, at 4,653.7.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was up 12.05 points, or 0.44 percent, at 2,739.69.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index ended up 19 points, or 0.51 percent, at 3,749.27. In later screen trade, the IBIS DAX ended up 47.0 points, or 1.26 percent, at 3,777.56.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $339.75 and silver finished two cents firmer at $4.75. Platinum ended $5.50 firmer at $415.50, while palladium finished $4.50 firmer at $198.50.
